column2: My mind moves me to tell of forms changed into new
bodies; gods, for you changed those too, on my undertakings
breathe, and from the first origin of the world
down to my own times draw out an unbroken song.
Before the sea and the lands and the sky that covers all,
there was one face of nature in the whole round world,
which they called chaos: a rough and unordered mass,
nothing but inert weight, and heaped in one place
the warring seeds of things not well joined.
No Titan yet gave light to the world,
nor did Phoebe renew her new horns by growing,
nor did the earth hang in the air poured round it,
balanced by its own weights, nor had Amphitrite
stretched out her arms along the long margin of the lands;
and where there was air, there too were earth and sea and ether.
So the earth was unstable, the water unswimmable,
the air lacking light: nothing kept its own form,
and one thing stood in the way of another, because in one body
cold things fought with hot, wet with dry,
soft with hard, things having weight with things without weight.
A god and a kinder nature settled this strife.
For he cut the lands off from the sky, and the waters from the lands,
and set the clear sky apart from the thick air.
When he had unrolled these and freed them from the blind heap,
he bound them, set apart in their places, in harmonious peace.
The fiery, weightless force of the vaulted sky
flashed out and made itself a place on the highest summit:
next to it in lightness and in place is air;
denser than these, the earth drew the large elements
and was pressed down by its own weight: the flowing water
took the outermost place and held in the solid globe.
When he, whichever of the gods he was, had so arranged
and cut up the mass and brought the cut parts into members,
first, so that it would not be unequal on any
side, he rolled the earth into the shape of a great ball.
Then he spread out the seas and ordered them to swell with rushing winds
and to surround the shores of the encircled earth.
He added springs too, and huge pools and lakes,
and girded the down-flowing rivers with slanting banks,
which, different in their places, are partly swallowed by the earth itself,
partly reach the sea and, received into the plain
of freer water, beat on shores instead of banks.
He ordered the plains to stretch out, the valleys to sink,
the woods to be covered with leaf, the stony mountains to rise.
And as two zones cut the sky on the right, and as many
on the left side, and a fifth is hotter than those,
so the care of the god marked off the enclosed load with the same number,
and as many regions are pressed on the earth.
Of these the one in the middle is not habitable for heat:
deep snow covers two: between both he placed as many
and gave them a temperate climate, flame mixed with cold.
Above these hangs the air, which, by as much as, than the weight of earth
and the weight of water, it is lighter, by so much is heavier than fire.
There he ordered mists, there clouds to settle,
and thunders that would move human minds,
and winds that make lightning flashes along with thunderbolts.
To these too the maker of the world did not allow
the air to hold everywhere: even now they are barely withstood,
though each one rules his blasts in a different tract,
from tearing the world apart: so great is the discord of the brothers.
Eurus withdrew to the Dawn and the Nabataean kingdoms
and Persia and the ridges set beneath the morning rays;
evening and the shores that grow warm with the setting sun
are nearest to Zephyrus: Scythia and the seven plough-oxen
bristling Boreas invaded: the opposite land
grows wet with constant clouds and rain from Auster.
Above these he placed the clear and weightless
ether, having nothing of earthly dregs.
Hardly had he so fenced off all things with fixed limits,
when the stars, which had long lain hidden pressed under that mass,
began to blaze out across the whole sky.
And so that no region should be bereft of its own living things,
the stars and the forms of the gods hold the heavenly ground,
the waters fell to the shining fish to be lived in,
the earth took the wild beasts, the mobile air the birds.
A creature holier than these and more capable of high mind
was still lacking, and one that could have dominion over the rest.
Man was born, whether that maker of things,
the source of a better world, made him from divine seed,
or the earth, new and only lately drawn away from the high
ether, still kept seeds of its kindred sky;
which the son of Iapetus, mixed with rain waters,
shaped into the likeness of the gods who govern all things.
And while the other animals, bent forward, look at the earth,
he gave man an uplifted face, and ordered him to see the sky
and to raise his upturned face to the stars.
So the earth, which had just been rough and without image,
changed, put on the unknown figures of men.
First the Golden Age was sown, which with no avenger,
of its own will, without law, kept faith and right.
Punishment and fear were absent, nor were threatening words read
on fixed bronze, nor did the suppliant crowd fear
the face of its judge, but they were safe without an avenger.
Not yet, cut down to visit a foreign world,
had the pine come down from its mountains into the clear waves,
and mortals knew no shores but their own.
Not yet did steep ditches gird the towns;
there was no trumpet of straight bronze, no horns of curved bronze,
no helmets, no sword: without the use of soldiers
the peoples, free from care, passed their gentle leisure.
The earth itself too, untaxed, untouched by the hoe, and wounded
by no ploughshares, gave all things of itself;
and content with foods created with no one compelling,
they gathered arbutus fruit and mountain strawberries
and cornel cherries and blackberries clinging to hard brambles,
and acorns that had fallen from the spreading tree of Jove.
Spring was eternal, and gentle zephyrs with warm breezes
caressed flowers born without seed.
Soon too the unploughed earth bore crops,
and the field, not renewed, grew white with heavy ears of grain;
now rivers of milk, now rivers of nectar flowed,
and yellow honey dripped from the green holm-oak.
After Saturn was sent into gloomy Tartarus
and the world was under Jove, the silver race came in,
worse than gold, more precious than tawny bronze.
Jupiter shortened the times of the old spring,
and through winters and summers and unequal autumns
and a brief spring he completed the year in four seasons.
Then for the first time the air, scorched with dry heats,
glowed white, and ice, bound by the winds, hung down.
Then for the first time they went into houses (the houses were caves
and dense thickets and twigs bound with bark).
Then for the first time the seeds of Ceres were buried in long furrows,
and bullocks, pressed by the yoke, groaned.
Third after that one came the bronze race,
fiercer in nature and readier for dreadful arms,
yet not wicked. The last is of hard iron.
At once into the age of the worse vein burst
every wrong: shame fled, and truth and faith;
into whose place came frauds and tricks
and plots and force and the wicked love of having.
The sailor gave sails to the winds (nor yet did he know them well);
and keels, which had long stood on the high mountains,
leapt upon unknown waves,
and the ground, common before like the light of the sun and the breezes,
the cautious surveyor marked with a long boundary.
Nor were only crops and owed food demanded
of the rich soil, but they went into the bowels of the earth:
and the riches which she had hidden away and moved near the Stygian shades
are dug up, incitements to evils.
And now harmful iron, and gold more harmful than iron,
had come forth: war comes forth, which fights with both,
and with bloody hand shakes clashing arms.
They live on plunder: guest is not safe from host,
nor father-in-law from son-in-law; even between brothers kindness is rare.
The husband threatens the death of his wife, she that of her husband;
terrible stepmothers mix pale aconites;
the son before his day inquires into his father's years.
Piety lies defeated, and the maiden, of the lands wet with slaughter,
Astraea, last of the heaven-dwellers, left the earth.
And so that the steep ether should be no safer than the lands,
they say the Giants aimed at the kingdom of heaven
and built up heaped mountains to the high stars.
Then the almighty father, with a hurled thunderbolt, shattered Olympus
and struck Pelion off from Ossa beneath it.
When the dreadful bodies lay crushed by their own mass,
they say that Earth, drenched with the abundant blood of her sons,
was soaked through and gave life to the warm gore,
and, so that no memorials of her stock should remain,
turned it into the shape of men. But that offspring too
was a scorner of the gods and most greedy for savage slaughter
and violent: you would know they were born from blood.
When the Saturnian father saw this from his highest citadel,
he groans, and, the deed being recent and not yet made known,
recalling the foul feasts of Lycaon's table,
he conceives in his mind huge wrath worthy of Jove,
and calls a council: no delay held back those called.
There is a lofty road, plain to see when the sky is clear:
it has the name Milky, notable for its very whiteness.
By this the gods go to the halls of the great Thunderer
and his royal house. On the right and left the halls
of the noble gods are thronged, their doors open
(the common folk live elsewhere): in this part the powerful
and famous heaven-dwellers have set their household gods.
This is the place which, if boldness be granted to my words,
I would not fear to have called the Palatine of great heaven.
So when the gods had sat down in the marble recess,
he himself, higher in place and leaning on his ivory sceptre,
three and four times shook the terrifying hair
of his head, with which he moved earth, sea and stars.
Then in such ways he opened his indignant lips:
“I was not more anxious for the kingdom of the world in that
time when each of the snake-footed ones was preparing
to throw his hundred arms upon the captive sky.
For though the enemy was fierce, still that war hung
on one body and from one origin.
Now, wherever Nereus sounds round the whole world,
I must destroy the mortal race: I swear by the rivers
below, gliding under the earth through the Stygian grove!
all things were tried first: but an incurable body
must be cut away with the sword, so that the sound part is not drawn in.
I have demigods, I have rustic powers, nymphs
and fauns and satyrs and mountain-dwelling silvani:
since we do not yet deem them worthy of the honour of heaven,
let us at least allow them to live in the lands we have given.
Or do you believe, O gods, that they will be safe enough,
when against me, who hold and rule the thunderbolt and you,
Lycaon, known for his savagery, has laid a plot?”
All roared together, and with burning zeal demand
the one who dared such things. So, when an impious band raged
to blot out the Roman name with Caesar's blood,
stunned by such great terror of sudden ruin
was the human race, and the whole world shuddered:
nor is the loyalty of your people less pleasing to you, Augustus,
than that was to Jove. After he with voice and hand
had checked the murmurs, all kept silence.
When the clamour stopped, pressed down by the ruler's weight,
Jupiter again broke the silence with this speech:
“He indeed has paid the penalty; put away this care.
But what was committed, and what the punishment is, I will tell.
The infamy of the times had reached our ears;
wishing it false, I glide down from highest Olympus
and, a god in human shape, I go over the lands.
It is a long delay to count how much wrong was found
everywhere: the infamy itself was less than the truth.
I had crossed Maenalus, dreadful with the lairs of wild beasts,
and with Cyllene the pine woods of cold Lycaeus:
from here the seat and inhospitable roof of the Arcadian tyrant
I enter, as the late twilight was drawing on the night.
I gave signs that a god had come, and the common people had begun
to pray: at first Lycaon mocks their pious prayers,
then says ‘I will test, by a clear trial, whether this
is a god or a mortal. Nor will the truth be doubtful.’
At night he prepares to destroy me, heavy with sleep,
by an unexpected death: this test of the truth pleases him.
Nor is he content with that: of a hostage sent from the Molossian people
he slit open the throat with a blade,
and so the half-dead limbs he partly softened in boiling
waters, partly roasted over a fire set under them.
As soon as he placed this on the table, I with avenging flame
overturned the roof onto household gods worthy of their master.
He himself flees in terror, and reaching the silence of the countryside
howls out and tries in vain to speak: from himself
his mouth gathers rage, and with his usual lust for slaughter
he turns on the flocks and even now rejoices in blood.
His clothes pass into shaggy hair, his arms into legs:
he becomes a wolf and keeps traces of his old form.
The greyness is the same, the same violence of face,
the same eyes shine, the same image of savagery.
One house has fallen. But not one house alone deserved
to perish: wherever the earth lies open, wild Erinys reigns.
You would think they had sworn to crime. Let all quickly pay
the penalties they have earned (so my judgement stands).”
Some approve Jove's words aloud and add goads to his raging,
others fill their part with assent.
Yet the loss of the human race is a grief
to all, and they ask what the form of the earth will be,
bereft of mortals, who will bring incense
to the altars, whether he means to hand the lands to wild beasts to ravage.
To those asking such things (for the rest would be his care)
the king of the gods forbids alarm, and promises offspring unlike
the former people, of wondrous origin.
And now he was about to scatter thunderbolts over all the lands:
but he feared that the sacred ether, from so many fires,
might catch flame and the long axis blaze up:
he recalls too that it is in the fates that a time will come
when sea, when earth, and the seized palace of heaven
will burn, and the besieged mass of the world will labour.
The weapons forged by the hands of the Cyclopes are put away:
a different punishment pleases, to destroy the mortal race beneath
the waves and send down rainstorms from all the sky.
At once he shuts Aquilo in the caves of Aeolus,
and whatever blasts put to flight the clouds drawn on,
and sends out Notus. Notus flies out on dripping wings,
his terrible face covered in pitch-black gloom:
his beard heavy with rain, water flows from his white hair;
mists sit on his brow, his wings and the folds of his robe drip.
And as with his hand he pressed the widely hanging clouds,
a crash comes: then thick rains pour down from the ether.
Juno's messenger, clothed in varied colours,
Iris draws up waters and brings nourishment to the clouds.
The crops are laid flat, and the farmer's lamented
hopes lie low, and the labour of the long year perishes in vain.
Nor is Jove's wrath content with his own sky, but him
his sea-blue brother helps with auxiliary waves.
He calls together the rivers. When they had entered the halls
of their tyrant, “There is no need of a long exhortation
now,” he says. “Pour out your strength:
so the work requires! Open your houses and, the dams removed,
let loose all the reins to your streams!”
He had ordered; they return and loosen the mouths of their springs
and roll into the seas in unbridled course.
He himself struck the earth with his trident: and it
trembled, and with the motion opened ways for the waters.
Spreading out, the rivers rush through the open plains
and with the crops they sweep away orchards together with flocks and men
and houses, and shrines with their sacred things.
If any house remained and could withstand so great an evil
unthrown, still a higher wave covers its roof,
and its towers lie hidden, pressed under the flood.
And now sea and earth had no distinction:
all things were sea; and the sea lacked shores too.
One takes a hill, another sits in a curved boat
and pulls the oars there where he lately ploughed,
one sails over crops or the roof of his sunken
farmhouse, one catches a fish in the top of an elm.
An anchor is fixed, if chance brought it, in a green meadow,
or curved keels graze the vineyards beneath;
and where just now slender goats cropped the grass,
there now shapeless seals lay down their bodies.
The Nereids wonder at groves and cities and houses under water,
and dolphins hold the woods and run into the high
branches and knock against the shaken oaks.
The wolf swims among the sheep, the wave carries tawny lions,
the wave carries tigers; neither does the strength of lightning help the boar,
nor swift legs the stag carried off.
And after long seeking lands where it could alight,
the wandering bird, its wings worn out, falls into the sea.
The boundless licence of the sea had buried the hills,
and new waves beat on the mountain peaks.
The greatest part is seized by the wave; those whom the wave spared,
long fasting with scant food overcomes.
Phocis parts the Aonians from the fields of Oeta,
a fertile land while it was land, but at that time
a part of the sea and a broad plain of sudden waters.
There a steep mountain seeks the stars with two peaks,
Parnassus by name, and its summits rise above the clouds.
When here Deucalion (for the sea had covered the rest),
carried in a small raft with the partner of his bed, ran aground,
they worship the Corycian nymphs and the powers of the mountain
and fate-telling Themis, who then held the oracles.
No man was better than he or more loving of justice,
nor any woman more reverent of the gods than she.
When Jupiter sees the world standing in liquid marshes,
and one man surviving out of so many thousands just now,
and sees one woman surviving out of so many thousands just now,
both innocent, both worshippers of the godhead,
he scattered the clouds and, the rainstorms removed by the north wind,
showed the lands to the sky and the ether to the lands.
Nor does the anger of the sea remain, and, laying down his three-pointed weapon,
the ruler of the sea soothes the waters, and calls sea-blue Triton,
standing out above the deep, his shoulders covered with native purple shells,
and orders him to blow into his sounding conch
and by the given signal now to recall
the waves and rivers. He takes up the hollow trumpet,
twisted, which grows wide in a spiral from its base,
the trumpet which, when it has taken in air in the middle of the sea,
fills with its voice the shores lying under either Phoebus.
Then too, as it touched the god's mouth, wet with his dripping beard,
and, blown, sang the ordered retreat,
it was heard by all the waters of land and sea,
and all the waters by which it was heard, it held back.
Now the sea has a shore, the channel holds full streams,
the rivers sink and the hills seem to come out,
the ground rises, places grow as the waters decrease,
and after a long day the woods show their bared
tops and keep mud left on their leaves.
The world was restored. When he saw it empty,
and the desolate lands keeping a deep silence,
Deucalion, tears welling up, thus addresses Pyrrha:
“O sister, O wife, O only woman surviving,
whom common kin and a cousin's origin joined to me,
then marriage, now dangers themselves join,
of the lands, all that the setting and the rising see,
we two are the crowd; the sea has taken the rest.
And even now this confidence in our life is not
certain enough; even now the clouds terrify my mind.
What heart would you have now, poor one, if without me
you had been snatched from the fates? In what way could you
bear fear alone? With whom consoling you would you grieve?
For I (believe me), if the sea held you too,
would follow you, wife, and the sea would hold me too.
O if only I could restore the peoples by my father's
arts and pour souls into moulded earth!
Now the mortal race remains in us two
(so it seemed good to the gods), and we remain as samples of men.”
He had spoken, and they wept. They resolved to pray to the heavenly
power and seek help through the sacred oracles.
There is no delay: together they go to the waters of Cephisus,
not yet clear, but already cutting their known course.
Then when they had sprinkled the drawn water
on their clothes and head, they turn their steps to the holy
goddess's shrine, whose gables were pale
with foul moss, and the altars stood without fires.
When they touched the temple's steps, each falls
face down on the ground and, trembling, gave kisses to the cold stone,
and so they said, “If divine powers, won over by just prayers,
grow soft again, if the anger of the gods is bent,
tell, Themis, by what art the loss of our race
may be repaired, and bring help, most gentle one, to drowned things.”
The goddess was moved and gave an oracle: “Go away from the temple
and veil your heads and loosen your girded clothes
and throw behind your back the bones of your great mother.”
They were stunned a long time, and Pyrrha first breaks the silence
with her voice and refuses to obey the goddess's orders,
and asks with fearful mouth that she give her pardon, and fears
to wound her mother's shade by throwing her bones.
Meanwhile they go over again the words of the given oracle,
dark with blind hiding places, and turn them over within themselves and between them.
Then the son of Prometheus, with calm words, the daughter of Epimetheus
soothes, and says: “Either my cleverness is deceitful,
or oracles are pious and urge no wrong.
The great parent is the earth; the stones in the body of the earth
I think are called bones; we are bidden to throw these behind our backs.”
Although the Titan's daughter was moved by her husband's reading,
still her hope is in doubt: so much do both
distrust the heavenly warnings. But what will it hurt to try?
They go apart, and veil their heads, and ungird their tunics,
and send the bidden stones behind their own footsteps.
The rocks (who would believe this, unless antiquity were witness?)
began to put off their hardness and their stiffness,
and to soften by delay, and, softened, to take on form.
Soon, when they had grown and a gentler nature
reached them, a certain, though not clear, form of a human
can be seen, but, as if begun from marble,
not finished enough, and most like rough statues.
Yet whatever part of them was moist with some juice
and earthy was turned to the use of a body;
what is solid and cannot bend is changed into bones;
what was just now a vein remained under the same name;
and in a short space, by the will of the gods, the stones
thrown by the man's hands took on the face of men,
and from the woman's throw woman was made anew.
Hence we are a hard race, and one that knows labours,
and we give proof from what origin we were born.
The other animals, in different forms, the earth
bore of her own accord, after the old moisture from the fire
of the sun grew hot, and the mud and the wet marshes
swelled with the heat, and the fertile seeds of things,
nourished in the living soil as in a mother's womb,
grew, and took on some shape by lingering.
So, when the seven-mouthed Nile has left the soaked fields
and given back its streams to their ancient bed,
and the fresh slime has blazed under the heavenly star,
the farmers, turning the clods, find very many animals,
and among these some just begun, at the very
moment of birth, some unfinished and lacking
their proper parts they see; and often in the same body
one part lives, the other part is raw earth.
For when moisture and heat have taken on a balance,
they conceive, and from these two all things arise;
and though fire is hostile to water, moist vapour creates
all things, and a discordant concord is fit for offspring.
So when the earth, muddy from the recent flood,
grew hot again under the heavenly suns and the deep heat,
she brought forth countless species, and partly figures
of old she restored, partly she created new monsters.
She did not wish it, indeed, but you too, greatest Python,
she bore then, and to the new peoples, unknown serpent,
you were a terror: so much space of the mountain you held.
Him the bow-bearing god, who had never used such weapons
before, except on deer and fleeing roe,
weighed down with a thousand shafts, his quiver almost emptied,
destroyed, the venom pouring out through the black wounds.
And lest age could blot out the fame of the deed,
he founded sacred games with a crowded contest,
called Pythian from the name of the serpent overcome.
Here, whoever of the young men with hand or feet or wheel
had won received the honour of oak leaves:
there was no laurel yet, and his temples, comely with long hair,
Phoebus wreathed from any tree at all.
Phoebus' first love was Daphne, daughter of Peneus, which not
blind chance gave, but the savage anger of Cupid.
The Delian, proud of late from the conquered serpent,
had seen him bending his horns with the string drawn back,
and “What have you to do, wanton boy, with mighty weapons?”
he had said; “those gear suit our shoulders,
who can give sure wounds to a beast, give wounds to an enemy,
who just now laid low the swollen Python, pressing so many acres
with his pestilent belly, with countless arrows.
You be content to stir up with your torch some loves or other
of yours, and do not lay claim to our praises.”
The son of Venus to him: “Your bow may pierce all things, Phoebus,
mine you,” he says, “and as much as all animals yield
to a god, by so much is your glory less than ours.”
He spoke, and, striking the air with beaten wings,
untiring, he stood on the shady peak of Parnassus,
and from his arrow-bearing quiver drew two shafts
of opposite works: this one drives love away, that one makes it.
The one that makes it is golden and gleams with a sharp point;
the one that drives away is blunt and has lead under the reed.
This one the god fixed in the nymph, Peneus' daughter, but with that one
he wounded Apollo's marrow, piercing through the bones.
At once the one loves, the other flees the name of lover,
rejoicing in the darkness of the woods and in the spoils
of captured beasts, and rival of the unwed Phoebe.
A ribbon held back her hair, set without order.
Many sought her; she, turning from her suitors,
impatient of and without a man, roams the pathless groves,
and cares not what Hymen, what Love, what marriages are.
Often her father said, “Daughter, you owe me a son-in-law”;
often her father said, “Child, you owe me grandsons”;
she, hating the marriage torches as if a crime,
is suffused on her beautiful face with a modest blush,
and clinging to her father's neck with coaxing arms,
“Give me, dearest father,” she said, “to enjoy
perpetual virginity: her father gave this before to Diana.”
He indeed complies, but that beauty of yours forbids you to be
what you wish. And your form fights against your prayer:
Phoebus loves, and desires marriage with Daphne, once seen,
and what he desires he hopes, and his own oracles deceive him.
And as light stubble burns when the ears are taken off,
as hedges blaze from torches which a traveller by chance
either brought too near or left behind at daybreak,
so the god went into flames, so in his whole breast
he burns, and by hoping feeds a barren love.
He looks at her unadorned hair hanging on her neck,
and says, “What if it were combed?” He sees, flashing with fire,
her eyes like stars, he sees her lips, which it is not
enough to have seen; he praises her fingers and hands
and arms, and her upper arms bare more than halfway.
Whatever is hidden, he thinks better. She flees swifter than the light
breeze, and does not stop at these words of his calling her back:
“Nymph, I pray, daughter of Peneus, stay! I do not pursue as an enemy:
nymph, stay! So the lamb flees the wolf, so the deer the lion,
so doves with trembling wing flee the eagle,
each its own enemies: love is my cause for following.
Wretched me! that you not fall headlong, or brambles mark
your legs that do not deserve to be hurt, and I be the cause of your pain!
Rough are the places where you hurry. More slowly, I beg,
run, and check your flight; I myself will follow more slowly.
Yet ask whom you please. I am not a dweller of the mountain,
I am not a shepherd, not here do I, shaggy, watch over
herds and flocks. You do not know, rash one, you do not know
whom you flee, and that is why you flee. The Delphic land
and Claros and Tenedos and the Pataran palace serve me,
Jupiter is my father; through me what will be and what was
and what is is revealed; through me songs harmonize with strings.
Sure indeed is our arrow, yet one arrow is
surer than ours, which has made wounds in my empty breast.
Medicine is my invention, and through the world I am called
the help-bringer, and the power of herbs is subject to us:
ah me, that love is curable by no herbs,
and the arts that help all do not help their master!”
As he was about to say more, Peneus' daughter with timid running
fled, and left with him his words unfinished,
even then seen as comely. The winds bared her body,
and the blasts meeting her fluttered her clothes against her,
and the light breeze sent her hair streaming back,
and her beauty was increased by flight. But the young god
no longer bears to waste his coaxing words, and, as Love
himself urged, follows her footsteps at full pace.
As when a Gallic hound in an empty field has seen a hare,
and this one seeks his prey with his feet, that one safety:
the one, like one about to fasten on, now, now hopes
to hold, and grazes her tracks with outstretched muzzle,
the other is in doubt whether she is caught, and from the very
bites is snatched away and leaves the touching mouth behind:
so are the god and the maiden; he swift with hope, she with fear.
Yet he who pursues, helped by the wings of Love,
is swifter and denies her rest, and over the back of the fleeing one
he hangs, and breathes on the hair scattered on her neck.
Her strength used up, she grew pale, and overcome
by the toil of swift flight, looking at Peneus' waters,
“Bring help, father,” she says, “if you rivers have divine power.
By changing it destroy the shape by which I pleased too much!”
Her prayer scarcely finished, a heavy numbness seizes her limbs:
her soft breast is girdled with thin bark,
her hair grows into leaves, her arms into branches,
her foot, just now so swift, clings with sluggish roots,
a treetop holds her face; her radiance alone remains in her.
This too Phoebus loves, and, his right hand placed on the trunk,
he feels the breast still trembling under the new bark,
and embracing the branches, like limbs, in his arms,
he gives kisses to the wood: yet the wood shrinks from the kisses.
To her the god said: “But since you cannot be my wife,
you will surely be my tree. Always will
my hair, my lyres, my quivers have you, laurel:
you will attend the Latin leaders, when the glad voice
sings triumph and the Capitol sees the long processions:
at Augustus' doorposts, the same most faithful guardian,
you will stand before the doors and guard the oak between,
and as my head is youthful with unshorn hair,
you too always wear the perpetual honours of your leaves.”
Paean had finished: the laurel, with her branches just made,
nodded, and seemed to have shaken her top like a head.
There is a grove of Haemonia which a steep wood closes in
on every side: they call it Tempe. Through it Peneus, poured
from the foot of Pindus, rolls with foaming waves,
and by its heavy fall gathers clouds that drive thin mists,
and sprinkles the treetops with spray
and wearies more than the neighbourhood with its sound.
This is the house, this the seat, this the inner shrine of the great
river; dwelling here in a cave made from rocks,
he gave laws to the waves and to the nymphs who dwell in the waves.
There first gather the rivers of his own country,
not knowing whether to congratulate or console the parent:
poplar-bearing Spercheus and restless Enipeus,
and old Apidanus, and gentle Amphrysus, and Aeas,
and soon other streams, which, wherever their impulse carried them,
lead down into the sea their waters weary with wandering.
Inachus alone is absent, and, hidden in the depth of his cave,
swells his waters with tears, and, most wretched, mourns his daughter Io
as lost. He does not know whether she enjoys life
or is among the shades; but her whom he finds nowhere
he thinks is nowhere, and in his mind fears worse things.
Jupiter had seen her returning from her father's
river, and “O maiden worthy of Jove, who will make some man or other
happy with your bed, seek,” he had said, “the shade
of the deep groves” (and he had pointed out the shade of the groves),
“while it is hot and the sun is highest in the middle of its circle.
But if you fear to enter the lairs of wild beasts alone,
safe with a god as guard, you will go into the secret places of the groves,
and no common god, but I, who hold the great heavenly
sceptre in my hand, I, who hurl the wandering thunderbolts.
Do not flee me!” for she was fleeing. Already the pastures of Lerna
and the Lyrcean fields planted with trees she had left behind,
when the god, drawing a fog over them, hid the wide lands,
and stopped her flight and ravished her chastity.
Meanwhile Juno looked down into the midst of the fields,
and wondered that flying mists had made the face of night
under the bright day; she sensed that they were not of a river,
nor sent up from the moist earth;
and she looks around for where her husband is, as one who
by now knew the thefts of a husband caught so many times.
When she did not find him in the sky, “Either I am deceived,
or I am wronged,” she says, and gliding down from the highest air
she stood on the earth and ordered the mists to withdraw.
He had foreseen his wife's coming, and into a shining
heifer he had changed the face of Inachus' daughter.
As a cow too she is beautiful. Saturn's daughter approves the cow's looks,
though unwilling, and asks also whose she is and from where
or from what herd, as if not knowing the truth.
Jupiter lies that she was born from the earth, so that the author
may stop being asked about. Saturn's daughter asks for her as a gift.
What should he do? It is cruel to hand over his love,
not to give her is suspicious. Shame it is that urges him on that side,
on this Love dissuades. Shame would have been beaten by Love;
but if a cow, a trifling gift, were refused to the partner of his race and bed,
it could seem to be no cow.
The rival handed over, the goddess did not at once put off all
her fear, and feared Jove, and was anxious about his theft,
until she gave her to Argus, son of Arestor, to be guarded.
Argus had a head ringed with a hundred eyes:
from these, two at a time in turn took rest,
the rest kept watch and stayed on guard.
However he had stood, he was looking at Io:
he had Io before his eyes, though turned away.
By daylight he lets her graze; when the sun is beneath the deep earth,
he shuts her in and puts chains around her undeserving neck.
She feeds on the leaves of trees and on bitter grass,
and instead of a bed, on the ground that does not always have grass
she lies, unhappy, and drinks muddy streams.
She too, when she wished to stretch out her arms as a suppliant to Argus,
had no arms to stretch out to Argus,
and, trying to complain, she gave out lowings from her mouth,
and was terrified at the sounds, and frightened by her own voice.
She came also to the banks where she often used to play,
the banks of Inachus; and when she saw in the water new
horns, she was terrified, and fled from herself in panic.
The Naiads do not know, and Inachus himself does not know,
who she is; but she follows her father, and follows her sisters,
and lets herself be touched, and offers herself to them as they wonder.
Old Inachus had held out grasses he had plucked:
she licks his hands and gives kisses to her father's palms,
and does not hold back her tears, and, if only words would follow,
she would beg for help and tell her name and her misfortunes.
Letters in place of words, which her hoof drew in the dust,
made the sad disclosure of her changed body.
“Wretched me!” cries father Inachus, and hanging on the horns
and the snowy neck of the moaning heifer,
“wretched me!” he repeats, “are you the daughter I sought through all
the lands? You, not found, were a lighter grief
than found. You are silent and return no words
in answer to ours, you only draw sighs from deep in your
breast, and, the one thing you can do, you low back at my words.
But I, unknowing, was preparing a bridal chamber and torches for you,
and my first hope was of a son-in-law, my second of grandsons.
Now you must have a husband from the herd, now a son from the herd.
Nor am I allowed to end such great griefs by death,
but being a god does harm, and the shut door of death
stretches our grief out into eternal ages?”
As he mourns so, starry Argus moves him away,
and drags off the daughter, snatched from her father, to other pastures.
He himself, far off, takes a high peak of a mountain,
from where, sitting, he watches in all directions.
And the ruler of the gods can no longer bear such great evils
of Phoroneus' descendant, and calls his son, whom the shining
Pleiad bore in childbirth, and orders him to give Argus to death.
There is little delay in taking wings for his feet and in his mighty hand
the sleep-bringing wand, and a cap for his hair.
When he had arranged these, Jove's son leaps down from his father's
citadel to the earth. There he took off his cap
and laid aside his wings; only the wand was kept.
With this, like a shepherd, through the out-of-the-way country, he drives goats,
which he has led off as he came, and he sings on reed pipes he has put together.
Caught by the new sound, Juno's guard says: “But you,
whoever you are, you could sit with me on this rock,”
Argus says, “for in no place is the grass richer
for the flock, and you see the shade is fit for shepherds.”
Atlas' grandson sat, and with much talking held back
the passing day with conversation, and by singing on the joined
reeds tries to conquer the watching eyes.
But he fights to overcome soft sleep,
and though slumber has been taken in by part of his eyes,
yet with part he stays awake. He asks too (for the pipe
had been found only lately) in what way it was found.
Then the god said: “On the cold mountains of Arcadia,
among the hamadryads of Nonacris the most famous
was a naiad; the nymphs called her Syrinx.
More than once she had escaped the satyrs following her,
and whatever gods the shady wood and the fertile
country hold. She worshipped the Ortygian goddess with her pursuits
and with virginity itself. Girt also in Diana's fashion,
she would deceive, and could be believed to be Latona's daughter, if
she did not have a bow of horn, if that one did not have one of gold.
Even so she deceived. As she returned from the Lycaean hill
Pan sees her and, his head wreathed with sharp pine,
speaks such words”—it remained to tell the words,
and that, the prayers scorned, the nymph fled through pathless places,
until she came to the calm stream of sandy Ladon;
that here, the waters hindering her course,
she begged her liquid sisters to change her,
and that Pan, when he thought he now had Syrinx caught,
held marsh reeds in place of the nymph's body;
and while he sighs there, the winds moved in the reed
made a thin sound, like one complaining;
that the god, captured by the new art and the sweetness of the voice,
said, “This union with you will remain to me!”
and so the reeds of unequal length, by a joining of wax
fixed to one another, kept the girl's name.
About to say such things, the Cyllenian saw that all
the eyes had sunk, and the lights were covered with sleep.
At once he checks his voice, and deepens the sleep,
stroking the drowsy eyes with the drugged wand.
Without delay, with his hooked sword he wounds him, nodding,
where the head borders the neck, and throws him, bloody,
off the rock, and stains the steep cliff with blood.
Argus, you lie low, and the light you had in so many lights
is put out, and one night takes over a hundred eyes.
Saturn's daughter takes them up, and on the feathers of her bird
sets them, and fills its tail with starry gems.
At once she blazed up, and did not put off the time of her anger,
and set before the eyes and mind of the Argive rival
a horror-bringing Fury, and hid blind goads in her breast,
and drove her in terror, a fugitive, through the whole world.
You were left, Nile, as the last of her immense toil.
As soon as she touched it, on the edge of the bank
she knelt down on her knees, and, lifted high with her neck thrown back,
raising her face, which alone she could, to the stars,
with groaning and tears and mournful lowing
she seemed to complain to Jove and beg for an end of her evils.
He, putting his arms around his wife's neck,
asks her to end the punishments at last, and “For the future
put away your fears,” he says; “never will she be a cause
of pain to you,” and bids the Stygian marshes hear this.
When the goddess is calmed, she takes on her former face
and becomes what she was before: the bristles flee from her body,
the horns shrink, the circle of the eye becomes narrower,
the gaping mouth is drawn in, shoulders and hands return,
and the hoof, parted into five nails, is used up:
nothing of the cow's form remains in her but whiteness.
And the nymph, content with the service of two feet,
stands upright, and fears to speak, lest she low
like a heifer, and timidly tries again her broken-off words.
Now, a goddess, she is worshipped, most famous, by the linen-wearing throng.
Now Epaphus is believed at last to have been born
from the seed of great Jove, and through the cities, joined with his mother,
he holds temples. Equal to him in spirit and in years
was Phaethon, sprung from the Sun. Him once, talking big,
not yielding to him, and proud of Phoebus as his parent,
the descendant of Inachus did not bear, and says: “Madman, you believe
your mother in everything, and are puffed up with the image of a false father.”
Phaethon blushed, and held back his anger with shame,
and carried Epaphus' insults to Clymene, his mother;
and says, “So that you may grieve more, mother, I, the free one,
I, the fierce one, kept silent. It shames us that these taunts
both could be spoken and could not be refuted.
But you, if indeed I am born of heavenly stock,
give a sign of so great a descent, and claim me for the sky.”
He spoke, and wrapped his arms around his mother's neck,
and by his own head and Merops' and his sisters' marriage torches
he begged her to give him signs of his true parent.
It is uncertain, Clymene, whether moved more by Phaethon's prayers or by anger
at the charge spoken against her, she stretched both arms
to the sky, and, looking up at the light of the sun,
“By this radiance,” she says, “marked with flashing rays,
son, I swear to you, by this which both hears and sees us,
that you, from this one you look on, from this one that rules the world,
sprung from the Sun. If I speak falsehoods, may he himself deny
that I may see him, and may that light be the last for our eyes.
Nor is it a long labour for you to know your father's home:
the house from which he rises borders on our land.
If only your mind moves you, go, and you will learn from him himself.”
At once Phaethon darts off, glad after such words
of his mother, and conceives the sky in his mind,
and passes his Ethiopians and the Indians set under the starry
fires, and, unwearied, goes to his father's rising-place.
